claim: "The ground bass is an eight-bar phrase... Across the whole song the bass pattern is heard roughly thirty-four times."
problem: The ground bass in Music for a While is three bars long, not eight. The standard Edexcel set-work analysis (Pearson's own support guide) counts it as heard roughly 4½ times in the tonic before modulating from bar 14, a three-bar reminder at bar 23, then a complete return at bar 29 heard a further three times before the close — around 9–10 statements in total. "Roughly thirty-four times" is impossible in a piece of this length (the piece runs to about 36 bars) and would cause a student to fail an identification question on the ground bass's length or repetition count.
correction: The ground bass is three bars long. It is heard about 4½ times in the tonic key before modulating (from bar 14), returns briefly in the original key at bar 23, then returns complete at bar 29 and is heard a further three times before the piece ends — roughly 9–10 statements overall, not 34.

claim: "What is the ground bass in Music for a While?" → "An eight-bar repeating bass phrase heard continuously throughout the piece, mostly conjunct with a descending shape."
problem: Repeats the same length error as the content field, but here it sits as the direct recall answer a student will memorise verbatim for the exam. The ground bass is three bars long, not eight.
correction: Change the flashcard answer to: "A three-bar repeating bass phrase heard throughout the piece, mostly conjunct (stepwise) with a rising-then-falling, arpeggio-based shape."

claim: "Listen too for the modulation partway through the song, where the music shifts up to a new key, lifting the energy for the final chorus — a very different, more sudden kind of harmonic movement compared with Purcell's continuously cycling ground bass."
problem: This describes a one-off 'gear-change' modulation reserved for the final chorus (like the classic pop semitone key-change). No such event occurs in Killer Queen. Per the official Edexcel/Pearson set-work analysis, every chorus (1, 2 and 3) modulates from the verse's C minor/E flat major to the same B flat major (the dominant) — it is a recurring feature of the song's structure, not a special event before the final chorus. The outro simply fades on an E flat major chord. A student repeating this claim in a tonality/structure answer would describe a modulation that isn't there.
correction: Remove the claim of a special late key change. Replace with: every chorus in Killer Queen modulates from the verse's C minor/E♭ major up to B♭ major (the dominant) in the same way each time — this recurring shift, not a one-off final-chorus modulation, is the harmonic device worth naming.

claim: "...Queen's multitrack studio production built through layered vocals and a late key change."
problem: Restates the same fabricated 'late key change' as the lesson's takeaway summary, so it is the line most likely to stick in a student's memory. As above, Killer Queen has no distinct late/final-chorus key change — the verse-to-chorus modulation (Eb major to Bb major) recurs identically at every chorus.
correction: Replace "a late key change" with wording such as "a recurring verse-to-chorus modulation" or drop the phrase entirely.

claim: "Killer Queen was the song that first hinted at this ambition reaching mainstream audiences: it became Queen's first UK Top 10 hit..."
problem: Factually wrong. Queen's actual first UK hit and first UK Top 10 single was "Seven Seas of Rhye" (reached #10 in April 1974), released months before Killer Queen. Killer Queen (released October 1974) reached #2 and was Queen's first UK Top 5 hit and first US hit — a bigger success, but not their first Top 10 hit. Background/context claims like this sit in the exact section (performing circumstances) that Component 3 context questions draw on.
correction: "Seven Seas of Rhye" was Queen's first UK Top 10 hit (#10, spring 1974). Killer Queen, released later that year, became their first UK Top 5 hit (peaking at #2) and first US hit — call it their breakthrough hit, not their first hit.

claim: "Killer Queen, written by Freddie Mercury, became the band's first major hit..."
problem: Same underlying error as the Lesson 4 finding, in vaguer form: Queen already had a hit single ("Seven Seas of Rhye", UK #10) months before Killer Queen. Describing Killer Queen as the band's "first major hit" is misleading even if not as precisely falsifiable as "first Top 10 hit."
correction: Reword to something like "became the band's commercial breakthrough" rather than "first major hit", since Seven Seas of Rhye preceded it as a Top 10 hit.

claim: "There are two main verses, each followed by a chorus... Between the second chorus and the final section comes a guitar solo played by Brian May... What makes the structure exam-worthy is the varied final section: rather than simply repeating the chorus again..."
problem: Undercounts the song's structure. Killer Queen has three verses and three choruses, not two: Verse 1 – Chorus 1 – instrumental link – Verse 2 – Chorus 2 (truncated) – guitar solo – Verse 3 – Chorus 3 (with added guitar) – outro. A full Verse 3 sits between the guitar solo and the final chorus; the lesson's "varied final section" glosses over an entire verse. A student who labels sections using this lesson's version would mislabel the guitar-solo-to-ending portion in a structure question.
correction: Killer Queen is Verse 1 – Chorus 1 – instrumental – Verse 2 – Chorus 2 (cut short) – guitar solo – Verse 3 – Chorus 3 – outro: three verses and three choruses, with Verse 3 occurring after the guitar solo and before the final chorus.

claim: "Identify the section of Killer Queen in which Brian May's guitar solo occurs." Mark scheme: "Award the mark for correctly naming the guitar solo section between the second chorus and the varied final section."
problem: The mark scheme encodes the same incomplete structure as the content field — it names only "the second chorus" and "the varied final section" as the guitar solo's neighbours, omitting that a full Verse 3 sits between the solo and the final (third) chorus. A student who correctly says the solo comes "between chorus 2 and verse 3" would not match this mark scheme's wording.
correction: Reword the mark scheme to accept the solo occurring "after chorus 2 and before verse 3 / the final chorus", reflecting that a third verse follows the solo before the final chorus.

claim: "Many listeners and analysts describe an underlying swung, compound-feel groove sitting against the song's notated simple-time pulse..."
problem: Gets the notated metre backwards. Per the official Edexcel/Pearson set-work analysis, Killer Queen is notated in 12/8 — compound quadruple time — with a swung feel; the compound metre IS the notated pulse, it is not a feel superimposed on a simple-time notation. A student asked to identify the time signature/metre would answer "simple time" based on this text and be wrong.
correction: Killer Queen is notated in compound quadruple time (12/8) with a swung, shuffling feel — the compound metre is the notated pulse itself, not a feel layered over simple time.

claim: "The scoring is deliberately modest: a solo voice, usually alto or countertenor in modern performances, accompanied only by basso continuo..."
problem: The official Edexcel/Pearson set-work guide describes the voice part as "most usually a tenor", and the specific edition set for study is scored for soprano. Countertenor performances exist and are well known (e.g. Alfred Deller) but are not the typical or prescribed voice type. This could mislead a voice-type identification answer.
correction: Music for a While is most often sung by tenor or soprano voice; the prescribed edition for this set work is scored for soprano. Countertenor recordings exist but are not the usual or exam-prescribed voice type.

claim: "The performing forces are a solo voice (originally likely a countertenor or alto voice for the stage production) accompanied by continuo..."
problem: Same issue as the Lesson 2 finding: the standard set-work guide describes the voice as "most usually a tenor", and the prescribed edition is soprano. Presenting countertenor/alto as the likely original voice type is speculative and inconsistent with the exam board's own guidance.
correction: Describe the voice as most usually tenor (with the prescribed edition scored for soprano), rather than speculating that the original stage voice was countertenor or alto.
